Reference: Midrigan and Xu (2014)

Model Setting

The paper asks how much financial frictions lower aggregate total factor productivity (TFP), and through which channel. Two channels are separated. First, frictions distort entry and technology adoption, so that too few producers operate the productive technology (the extensive margin). Second, frictions create dispersion in the returns to capital across producers that already operate, which is misallocation in the sense of Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) and Hsieh and Klenow (2009) (the intensive margin). The model is an extension of the establishment dynamics model of Hopenhayn (1992) with two sectors. Producers in the unproductive traditional sector use only labor and need no finance. Producers in the productive modern sector need two kinds of capital: a one-time sunk investment to enter, and physical capital to produce. Finance is limited by simple constraints on the amount of debt and equity a producer can issue.

The model is parameterized with plant-level data from Korean manufacturing (1991-1996), and its predictions are compared with plant-level data from China and Colombia, two countries with much less developed financial markets. The main finding is that financial frictions can reduce TFP, output and consumption substantially (output by up to 40 percent), but the bulk of the loss comes from the extensive margin. TFP losses from the misallocation of capital among modern-sector producers are small, at most about 5 percent in an open economy and 10 percent in a closed economy, which is one-eighth to one-fourth of the roughly 40 percent losses that Hsieh and Klenow (2009) document for China and India. The mechanism that undoes misallocation is self-financing: efficient producers accumulate internal funds and quickly grow out of their borrowing constraints, and the transitory productivity shocks measured in the data are too small to push capital far from its efficient level. Entry and adoption, in contrast, are large long-lived investments that pay off only gradually and are hard to finance from the modest profits of the traditional sector.

Profits, output and the optimal inputs are homogeneous of degree one in (A,exp⁡(z))(A,\exp(z))(A,exp(z)), so all variables are rescaled by exp⁡(z)\exp(z)exp(z). Let μ(a,e)\mu(a,e)μ(a,e) be the multiplier on the borrowing constraint. An extra unit of net worth relaxes the constraint by 1/(1−θ)1/(1-\theta)1/(1−θ) units of capital, and the producer keeps the fraction 1−θχ1-\theta\chi1−θχ of the additional profits, so the net worth accumulation decision satisfies:

1c(a,ei)=β∑jfi,j[(1+r)+1−θχ1−θμ(a′,ej)]1c(a′,ej)(13)\frac{1}{c(a,e_i)}=\beta\sum_jf_{i,j}\left[(1+r)+\frac{1-\theta\chi}{1-\theta}\mu(a',e_j)\right]\frac{1}{c(a',e_j)} \tag{13}c(a,ei​)1​=βj∑​fi,j​[(1+r)+1−θ1−θχ​μ(a′,ej​)]c(a′,ej​)1​(13)

The expectation that the constraint will bind in the future raises the return to saving above rrr and makes the producer accumulate net worth. The choices of labor and capital satisfy:

The marginal product of labor is equalized across producers, while the marginal product of capital equals the shadow cost of funds r+μ(a,e)r+\mu(a,e)r+μ(a,e) plus depreciation. Dispersion in net worth and productivity therefore produces dispersion in the marginal product of capital, which is the source of misallocation. The permanent component zzz does not appear in the rescaled problem: a producer that is twice as productive and has twice the assets is equally constrained. The decision rules show that the shadow cost of funds falls with net worth and is higher for more productive producers at a given net worth, that poor producers save to relax future constraints, and that rich producers dissave because they are impatient relative to the interest rate. Absent entry and productivity shocks the distribution of net worth would converge to a mass point with no dispersion in returns, so entry (new producers with little net worth) and transitory shocks are the only sources of misallocation.

Since modern-sector producers can borrow against intangible capital, their net worth can be negative. Debt is uncontingent, however, so the producer also faces the natural borrowing limit:

Even with θ=1\theta=1θ=1 a producer may therefore delay entry until it has saved enough, and equity, which makes repayments state-contingent, is critical for an efficient rate of entry. The entry rule is a threshold: a producer enters when its net worth and productivity are high enough, and the required productivity rises steeply as net worth falls towards about one (in units of exp⁡(z)\exp(z)exp(z)).

The one-for-one mapping relies on the assumption that financial frictions are the only source of dispersion in yi/kiy_i/k_iyi​/ki​; with technological differences or markups the formula overstates the losses caused by finance, and the paper calls the result of applying it to such environments or to data the measured TFP losses.

The first-best allocation also chooses the allocation of producers across sectors. A planner constrained only by the resource constraint and the technologies chooses KKK, the measures niτn^\tau_iniτ​ and nimn^m_inim​ and the labor allocation LτL^\tauLτ and LmL^mLm to maximize:

(∑iexp⁡(ei)niτ)1−η(Lτ)η+(∑iexp⁡(ei+ϕ)nim)1−η((Lm)αK1−α)η−(δ+γβ−1)K−∑inimβ(γ−1)κ(27)\left(\sum_i\exp(e_i)n^\tau_i\right)^{1-\eta}\left(L^\tau\right)^\eta+\left(\sum_i\exp(e_i+\phi)n^m_i\right)^{1-\eta}\left(\left(L^m\right)^\alpha K^{1-\alpha}\right)^\eta-\left(\delta+\frac{\gamma}{\beta}-1\right)K-\frac{\sum_in^m_i}{\beta}(\gamma-1)\kappa \tag{27}(i∑​exp(ei​)niτ​)1−η(Lτ)η+(i∑​exp(ei​+ϕ)nim​)1−η((Lm)αK1−α)η−(δ+βγ​−1)K−β∑i​nim​​(γ−1)κ(27)

subject to Lτ+Lm=1L^\tau+L^m=1Lτ+Lm=1 and the restrictions that the transition probabilities fi,jf_{i,j}fi,j​ impose on the measures. The objective is output of the two sectors minus the user cost of capital and the sunk cost of entry; the planner can reallocate consumption freely and so discounts at β/γ\beta/\gammaβ/γ.

Calibration

The data are the Korean manufacturing survey of plants with more than five workers, 1991-1999; the years 1991-1996 are used for the parameterization. The period is one year. Assigned parameters are γ=1.08\gamma=1.08γ=1.08 (real manufacturing output grew 8 percent per year), β=0.92γ\beta=0.92\gammaβ=0.92γ (an effective discount factor β/γ\beta/\gammaβ/γ of 0.92), δ=0.06\delta=0.06δ=0.06, η=0.85\eta=0.85η=0.85 and α=2/3\alpha=2/3α=2/3. Worker efficiency takes the values 0 and 1, with probabilities λ0=0.5\lambda_0=0.5λ0​=0.5 and λ1=0.79\lambda_1=0.79λ1​=0.79 of remaining in each state, so that 70 percent of workers supply labor. The modern sector's productivity advantage is ϕ=0.2/(1−η)\phi=0.2/(1-\eta)ϕ=0.2/(1−η), a 20 percent efficiency gap, which makes modern producers about 8 times larger in output and profits and 5 times larger in employment than traditional ones; values of ϕ\phiϕ equal to 0 and 0.4/(1−η)0.4/(1-\eta)0.4/(1−η) are also studied.

The remaining parameters are calibrated jointly. The transitory component is an AR(1) process with persistence ρ\rhoρ and innovation standard deviation σε\sigma_\varepsilonσε​, discretized with the Rouwenhorst method. These two parameters and the variance of zzz match the standard deviation of log output (1.31) and of output growth (0.59) and the autocorrelation of output at one, three and five years (0.90, 0.87, 0.85), with output measured as value added. The result is ρ=0.25\rho=0.25ρ=0.25, σε=0.50\sigma_\varepsilon=0.50σε​=0.50 and a variance of zzz of 1.47: because the autocorrelation decays much more slowly than geometrically, 85 percent of the cross-sectional variance of productivity is permanent. The collateral parameter θ=0.86\theta=0.86θ=0.86 and the equity parameter χ=0.10\chi=0.10χ=0.10 match a debt-to-output ratio of 1.2 and an equity-to-output ratio of 0.3 in Korean manufacturing. The entry cost κ=1.19\kappa=1.19κ=1.19 matches a ratio of intangible investment to value added of 4.6 percent; it is about 30 times traditional-sector profits and 4 times modern-sector profits. Among untargeted moments, the model reproduces the volatility and persistence of capital and employment and the fact that plants aged 1 to 5 grow about 0.11 faster than plants older than 10 (0.09 in the model), which requires equity issuance at entry; it predicts too few young plants (32 percent younger than five years against 51 percent in the data).

Quantitative Results

In the economy calibrated to Korea, finance hardly matters: 17 percent of modern producers are constrained, the capital-output ratio is 2.59 against (1−α)η/(r+δ)=2.65(1-\alpha)\eta/(r+\delta)=2.65(1−α)η/(r+δ)=2.65 without frictions, misallocation losses are 0.3 percent, and all entrants finance the sunk cost with equity and enter after one period, so the fraction of producers in the modern sector is 1/γ=0.931/\gamma=0.931/γ=0.93. Compared with the first best, the main distortion is over-investment: the interest rate is 4.7 percent instead of (β/γ)−1−1=8.7(\beta/\gamma)^{-1}-1=8.7(β/γ)−1−1=8.7 percent because of precautionary saving, the capital-output ratio is about 35 percent higher, and consumption is about 2 percent lower.

  • Open economy, lowering θ\thetaθ with χ=0.10\chi=0.10χ=0.10: as θ\thetaθ falls from 1 to 0 at an interest rate of 4.7 percent, the debt-to-output ratio falls from 1.3 to −0.6-0.6−0.6, the fraction of constrained producers rises to 83 percent, and modern-sector TFP falls from about 1 to 0.83. Misallocation losses are 1.4, 3.9, 4.4 and 4.7 percent at θ\thetaθ equal to 0.75, 0.50, 0.25 and 0, about one quarter of the TFP decline. The fraction of producers in the modern sector falls from 0.93 to 0.35, consumption falls by about 18 percent and output by about 40 percent.

  • No equity: with χ=0\chi=0χ=0 the outcomes at θ\thetaθ equal to 1 and 0 are the same, but at θ=0.75\theta=0.75θ=0.75 the fraction of modern producers is 0.61 instead of 0.93 and modern TFP and consumption are about 7 percent lower, while misallocation rises only from 1.4 to 2.7 percent.

  • Closed economy: the interest rate falls as constraints tighten (to −0.06-0.06−0.06 without external finance), which raises the desired capital of unconstrained producers and lengthens the time young producers need to catch up. Maximal misallocation losses double to about 10 percent (9.8 percent), and the variance of the marginal product of capital is 0.30 instead of 0.14. Without external finance 29 percent of producers are in the modern sector, modern TFP is 0.766, consumption 0.71 and output 1.06, against 1.00 and 1.69 with θ=1\theta=1θ=1.

  • Productivity gap: with ϕ=0\phi=0ϕ=0 misallocation is at most 0.4 percent and consumption barely changes although few producers enter. With a 40 percent gap, misallocation without finance is 9 percent, consumption is about 35 percent below the Korean calibration, and only 28 percent of producers are in the modern sector.

The asymmetry between the two margins reflects self-financing. A modern-sector producer earns high returns on internal funds while constrained, so it saves and outgrows the constraint within a few years; the residual dispersion in returns comes from young producers and from transitory shocks, both of which are limited. A traditional-sector producer must instead finance a sunk cost that is about 30 times its annual profits, and the larger the productivity gap, the more valuable the entry that is forgone.

Extensions: Technology Adoption and Exit

In the first extension a modern-sector producer can adopt a better technology by paying a fixed cost κp\kappa_pκp​:

Yt=exp⁡(z+et+ϕ+ϕp)1−η(LtαKt1−α)η(28)Y_t=\exp\left(z+e_t+\phi+\phi_p\right)^{1-\eta}\left(L_t^\alpha K_t^{1-\alpha}\right)^\eta \tag{28}Yt​=exp(z+et​+ϕ+ϕp​)1−η(Ltα​Kt1−α​)η(28)

with ϕp=0.27/(1−η)\phi_p=0.27/(1-\eta)ϕp​=0.27/(1−η), the lifetime productivity growth of Korean plants, and κp=exp⁡(ϕp)κ\kappa_p=\exp(\phi_p)\kappaκp​=exp(ϕp​)κ (calibrated values κ=0.30\kappa=0.30κ=0.30, κp=1.83\kappa_p=1.83κp​=1.83, θ=0.78\theta=0.78θ=0.78, χ=0.08\chi=0.08χ=0.08). Setting θ=0\theta=0θ=0 in an open economy lowers consumption by about 0.35 log points, output by 0.47 and modern TFP by 0.26. The fraction of producers with the productive technology falls from 0.86 to 0.18, while misallocation losses are 6.3 percent.

In the second extension a modern producer pays a fixed operating cost FFF in units of labor each period, or uses the traditional technology instead, so that its budget constraint becomes:

c+a′=max⁡[πm(a,ei)−WF,πτ(ei)]+(1+r)a(29)c+a'=\max\left[\pi^m(a,e_i)-WF,\pi^\tau(e_i)\right]+(1+r)a \tag{29}c+a′=max[πm(a,ei​)−WF,πτ(ei​)]+(1+r)a(29)

The entry cost is paid only once. Matching the share of young plants requires F=0.27F=0.27F=0.27 (9.4 percent of modern-sector labor), under which 26 percent of modern producers stop operating each period; the other calibrated values are σε=0.96\sigma_\varepsilon=0.96σε​=0.96, ρ=0.40\rho=0.40ρ=0.40, κ=2.66\kappa=2.66κ=2.66, θ=0.68\theta=0.68θ=0.68 and χ=0\chi=0χ=0. Without external finance misallocation is 4.1 percent, below the 4.7 percent of the benchmark, because the most constrained producers exit. The two extensions also change the micro implications. In the benchmark, removing external finance lowers the standard deviation of output growth from 0.58 to 0.32 (frictions act like an adjustment cost), raises the gap in the average product of capital between plants aged 1 to 5 and plants older than 10 from 0.08 to 0.73 log points, and raises the relative growth of young plants from 0.09 to 0.12. With adoption or exit, tighter constraints instead lower the relative growth of young plants.

Economy without Entry and Robustness

To isolate capital misallocation, an economy without entry in which all producers are in the modern sector is recalibrated to the same output moments and debt ratio (θ=0.57\theta=0.57θ=0.57, σε=0.83\sigma_\varepsilon=0.83σε​=0.83). Misallocation losses are 2.5 percent for the Korean calibration and 3.4 percent in an open economy without external finance. Tripling the volatility of shocks raises the losses to 5.6 and 20.3 percent (30 percent in a closed economy), and raising ρ\rhoρ to 0.9 raises the no-finance loss to 8.2 percent, but both variants contradict the output moments. A bound on the losses from the inability to adjust capital is obtained by assuming that capital does not respond to shocks at all:

worst TFP losses=(1−η)log⁡∫exp⁡(ei)−(1−αη)log⁡∫exp⁡(ei)1−η1−αη=12(1−α)η1−αη(1−η)σe2(30)\begin{aligned} \text{worst TFP losses}&=(1-\eta)\log\int\exp(e_i)-(1-\alpha\eta)\log\int\exp(e_i)^{\frac{1-\eta}{1-\alpha\eta}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\frac{(1-\alpha)\eta}{1-\alpha\eta}(1-\eta)\sigma_e^2 \end{aligned} \tag{30}worst TFP losses​=(1−η)log∫exp(ei​)−(1−αη)log∫exp(ei​)1−αη1−η​=21​1−αη(1−α)η​(1−η)σe2​​(30)

where the second line holds when eie_iei​ is normally distributed with unconditional variance σe2\sigma_e^2σe2​. With σe2=0.76\sigma_e^2=0.76σe2​=0.76 the bound is 3.7 percent, close to the 3.4 percent without external finance: frictions do prevent capital from adjusting, but the shocks are too small for this to matter. With shocks three times as volatile the bound is 33 percent.

Further variants are recalibrated to the same moments. With capital chosen before productivity is known, losses due to finance are 0.9 and 0.8 percent, although the formula based on the dispersion of yi/kiy_i/k_iyi​/ki​ gives measured losses of about 10 percent, which a planner facing the same technological constraint could not avoid. With prices set before productivity is known (variable markups) the losses are 0.3 and 1.1 percent; with an elasticity of substitution between capital and labor of 0.25 they are 1.5 and 3.2 percent; with capital-specific shocks 0.3 and 1.1 percent. Heterogeneity across three equally sized groups changes little: labor elasticities of 0.44, 0.66 and 0.89 give 2.6 and 2.9 percent (measured losses of 8.2 percent are mostly efficient dispersion); returns to scale of 0.55, 0.85 and 0.95 give 1.1 and 1.5 percent; collateral parameters of 0.15, 0.58 and 0.85 give 1.8 percent; and borrowing rates of 5, 10 and 15 percent without collateral constraints, calibrated to China, give 1.6 percent, because producers facing high rates accumulate internal funds, face a shadow cost of about 8 percent, and have an average product of capital only about 23 percent higher.

Evidence on Misallocation

Misallocation in the model works through an age channel (young producers have low net worth) and an adjustment channel (constrained producers cannot respond to shocks). The age channel is measured by projecting log⁡(Yi/Ki)\log(Y_i/K_i)log(Yi​/Ki​) on a full set of age dummies and applying the TFP loss formula to the fitted values. In the benchmark without external finance, age accounts for 3.7 of the 4.7 percent; in the model with exit, for 0.7 of 4.1 percent. In plant-level data, the measured TFP losses are large and similar across countries with very different financial development: 16.2 percent in Korea, 22.4 percent in China (1998-2007) and 17.7 percent in Colombia (1985-1990), whose ratios of debt to value added (to GDP for Colombia) are 1.2, 0.7 and about 0.2. The part due to age is 0.2, 0.3 and 2.7 percent, and the average product of capital of young plants relative to old ones is 0.21, 0.15 and −0.25-0.25−0.25. The variance of the transitory productivity component is 0.35, 0.30 and 0.24, so the worst-case losses from non-adjustment are 2.4, 2.9 and 1.9 percent. Measured losses are also about as large among old plants as among young plants. Finance therefore cannot account for the bulk of measured misallocation.

During the Korean crisis of 1997-1998 the debt-to-equity ratio of manufacturing fell from about four to two. A permanent fall in θ\thetaθ that reproduces this decline, in an open economy without equity, raises misallocation losses by about 5 percent on impact, which are partly reversed as producers accumulate funds, and lowers the number of modern producers by about 30 percent in the long run; TFP falls by about 5 percent on impact and 6.5 percent in the new steady state, of which 4.2 percent is the fall in first-best TFP. In the data TFP fell by 8 percent from 1996 to 1998, of which 6 percent reflects a 20 percent fall in the number of producers, and misallocation losses reached about 5 percent by 1999.

The note keeps the equation as printed in the paper, and its arguments are loose. The objective is steady-state output of the two sectors, per unit of the trend γt\gamma^tγt, net of the cost of the two kinds of capital. Start with the output terms. Next the cost of capital. Let lower-case letters denote variables divided by γt\gamma^tγt. The resource constraint (22) in these units, and the planner's objective with discount factor β\betaβ on rescaled consumption (which is the discount factor β/γ\beta/\gammaβ/γ on levels mentioned in the note), are

max⁡∑tβtlog⁡ct,ct+γkt+1−(1−δ)kt+xt=yt\max\sum_t\beta^t\log c_t,\qquad c_t+\gamma k_{t+1}-(1-\delta)k_t+x_t=y_tmaxt∑​βtlogct​,ct​+γkt+1​−(1−δ)kt​+xt​=yt​

The first-order condition for kt+1k_{t+1}kt+1​ in a steady state is

γc=βc(∂y∂k+1−δ)⟹∂y∂k=δ+γβ−1\frac{\gamma}{c}=\frac{\beta}{c}\left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial k}+1-\delta\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\partial y}{\partial k}=\delta+\frac{\gamma}{\beta}-1cγ​=cβ​(∂k∂y​+1−δ)⟹∂k∂y​=δ+βγ​−1

This is the same condition as that of maximizing output minus (δ+γβ−1)K\left(\delta+\frac{\gamma}{\beta}-1\right)K(δ+βγ​−1)K, the third term of the target: the user cost of capital at the planner's interest rate γ/β−1\gamma/\beta-1γ/β−1, which is 8.7 percent in the calibration.

The last term charges for entry. If the measure of modern producers is nm=∑inimn^m=\sum_in^m_inm=∑i​nim​ per unit of γt\gamma^tγt, their number grows at rate γ\gammaγ, so each period (γ−1)nm(\gamma-1)n^m(γ−1)nm new producers pay κ\kappaκ. The cost is paid one period before the new producers operate, so it is carried forward at the planner's gross rate γ/β\gamma/\betaγ/β and expressed relative to next period's trend, which is larger by γ\gammaγ:

γβ⋅(γ−1)nmκγ=∑inimβ(γ−1)κ\frac{\gamma}{\beta}\cdot\frac{(\gamma-1)n^m\kappa}{\gamma}=\frac{\sum_in^m_i}{\beta}(\gamma-1)\kappaβγ​⋅γ(γ−1)nmκ​=β∑i​nim​​(γ−1)κ

which is the printed term, and completes the target. The maximization is subject to Lτ+Lm=1L^\tau+L^m=1Lτ+Lm=1 and to the restrictions that the transition probabilities fi,jf_{i,j}fi,j​ place on the measures.

A caveat on this last term. The sunk investment is a stock, like capital with zero depreciation: in rescaled units xt=κ(γnt+1m−ntm)x_t=\kappa\left(\gamma n^m_{t+1}-n^m_t\right)xt​=κ(γnt+1m​−ntm​). Treating nt+1mn^m_{t+1}nt+1m​ exactly as kt+1k_{t+1}kt+1​ above, the first-order condition is

γκc=βc(∂y∂nm+κ)⟹∂y∂nm=(γβ−1)κ\frac{\gamma\kappa}{c}=\frac{\beta}{c}\left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial n^m}+\kappa\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\partial y}{\partial n^m}=\left(\frac{\gamma}{\beta}-1\right)\kappacγκ​=cβ​(∂nm∂y​+κ)⟹∂nm∂y​=(βγ​−1)κ

so the charge per modern producer that is consistent with the treatment of KKK would be (γβ−1)κ\left(\frac{\gamma}{\beta}-1\right)\kappa(βγ​−1)κ and not γ−1βκ\frac{\gamma-1}{\beta}\kappaβγ−1​κ. The printed coefficient is smaller by 1−ββκ\frac{1-\beta}{\beta}\kappaβ1−β​κ: it applies the interest factor to the flow of entry costs but omits the interest forgone on the existing stock. The note reproduces the paper faithfully, and the gap is small in the calibration (β=0.92γ=0.9936\beta=0.92\gamma=0.9936β=0.92γ=0.9936, so 0.08050.08050.0805 against 0.08700.08700.0870 per unit of κ\kappaκ), but the printed term could not be reproduced exactly from the stated environment.

This is the technology available in the first extension to a modern producer that has paid a second sunk cost κp\kappa_pκp​ (in units of exp⁡(z)\exp(z)exp(z)) to adopt a better technology. It is the modern technology of equation (3) with log productivity raised by a further ϕp>0\phi_p>0ϕp​>0; everything else, including the span of control η\etaη, the labor share parameter α\alphaα and the rescaling by exp⁡(z)\exp(z)exp(z), is unchanged. A producer now moves through up to three stages, traditional, modern, and modern with the better technology, and each upgrade is a discrete investment subject to the same collateral and equity constraints.

The values are ϕp=0.27/(1−η)\phi_p=0.27/(1-\eta)ϕp​=0.27/(1−η), chosen to match the lifetime productivity growth of Korean plants, and κp=exp⁡(ϕp)κ\kappa_p=\exp(\phi_p)\kappaκp​=exp(ϕp​)κ. Their meaning is easiest to see in terms of scale. From equation (23), the output, capital and profits of an unconstrained producer are proportional to exp⁡(e+ϕ+ϕp)\exp(e+\phi+\phi_p)exp(e+ϕ+ϕp​), so adoption multiplies the scale of the producer by

exp⁡(ϕp)=exp⁡(0.270.15)=exp⁡(1.8)≈6.05\exp(\phi_p)=\exp\left(\frac{0.27}{0.15}\right)=\exp(1.8)\approx6.05exp(ϕp​)=exp(0.150.27​)=exp(1.8)≈6.05

while the term in front of the input bundle rises by exp⁡(ϕp)1−η=exp⁡(0.27)≈1.31\exp(\phi_p)^{1-\eta}=\exp(0.27)\approx1.31exp(ϕp​)1−η=exp(0.27)≈1.31. Setting κp=exp⁡(ϕp)κ\kappa_p=\exp(\phi_p)\kappaκp​=exp(ϕp​)κ keeps the cost of adoption proportional to the scale it gives access to: with κ=0.30\kappa=0.30κ=0.30 this is 0.30×6.05≈1.80.30\times6.05\approx1.80.30×6.05≈1.8, the value 1.83 reported in the note up to rounding. The purpose of the extension is to add an investment that incumbents, and not only entrants, must finance, so that the extensive margin operates within the modern sector as well.

This is the budget constraint of a producer that has already paid the entry cost, in the extension with a fixed operating cost. It replaces equation (10). Each period the producer compares two ways of using its permanent productivity: operating the modern technology, which yields πm(a,ei)\pi^m(a,e_i)πm(a,ei​) from equation (11) minus the fixed cost of FFF units of labor, valued at the wage WWW; or operating the traditional technology, which yields πτ(ei)\pi^\tau(e_i)πτ(ei​) from equation (16) and requires neither capital nor the fixed cost. The choice is static, because the entry cost κ\kappaκ is not paid again and a producer can return to the modern technology at no cost, so the producer simply takes the maximum of the two profit flows. The rest of the constraint, c+a′c+a'c+a′ on the left and the gross return (1+r)a(1+r)a(1+r)a on net worth on the right, is as in equation (10).

The modern technology is used when

πm(a,ei)−πτ(ei)≥WF\pi^m(a,e_i)-\pi^\tau(e_i)\geq WFπm(a,ei​)−πτ(ei​)≥WF

Both profit flows increase with eie_iei​, but modern profits do so faster and also increase with net worth for a constrained producer. Low-productivity and poorly capitalized producers therefore suspend modern operations. This selection is why the note reports lower misallocation here than in the benchmark: the producers with the highest shadow cost of funds are the ones that leave the set MMM over which equation (25) is computed.

The factor 1−θχ1-\theta\chi1−θχ of equation (10) is absent from the profit term. This is consistent only because the note reports χ=0\chi=0χ=0 for this extension, so that no outside equity exists; with χ>0\chi>0χ>0 the term in brackets would be multiplied by 1−θχ1-\theta\chi1−θχ.
